extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners / attorneys who practice before the USPTO and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing ethical conduct, competence, communications, conflicts, investigative powers, burden of proof, sanctions, and appeal procedures for practitioners who practice before the USPTO. Includes both the USPTO Rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.xxx) and pre-2013 USPTO Code provisions (37 C.F.R. pt. 10) as applied in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to . . . [e]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers acts such as fabricating emails or altering documents to mislead an employer, client, tribunal or disciplinary body. Precedent examples cited include In re Lane and In re Slaughter. A finding may be based on admissions and documentary evidence showing deceit or falsification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct reflecting adversely on fitness — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule prohibiting conduct that reflects adversely on a practitioner's fitness to practice law before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where practitioner behavior (even outside direct client work) undermines confidence in practitioner’s ability to practice; often charged along with dishonesty-based violations when conduct shows poor fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence — 37 C.F.R. § 11.101
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation. Failure to timely file, to secure priority dates, or to pursue required petitions can constitute incompetence in patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence — 37 C.F.R. § 11.103
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes timely responses to USPTO deficiency notices, filing required petitions (e.g., petitions to restore priority or revive applications), paying required fees, and otherwise pursuing prosecution steps so as not to abandon client rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications / Keeping client informed — 37 C.F.R. § 11.104
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must keep a client reasonably informed and consult regarding the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to promptly and reasonably inform client of filing irregularities, abandonment notices, or options to revive/reinstate applications is a breach. The ALJ relied on emails, admissions, and timing to evaluate this obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal — 37 C.F.R. § 11.303
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or offer evidence known to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied when a practitioner makes false representations in court or tribunal proceedings; also invoked for false statements in disciplinary or adjudicative contexts (e.g., lying to the BBO or OED).

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements / failure to correct misapprehension in disciplinary matters — 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(a),(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of material fact, or knowingly fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a known misapprehension, in connection with a disciplinary matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers lies or omissions to investigative bodies, tribunals, or disciplinary agencies. The ALJ used this rule to evaluate statements to the BBO and OED about whether the client had been timely informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest / business transactions with client — 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(a) (and pre-2013 10.62, 10.65)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not enter into a business transaction with a client or acquire an interest adverse to a client without full disclosure and the client’s informed consent in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting ownership (stock/LLC interest) as compensation requires written disclosure of the risks and obtaining informed consent; failure to obtain written informed consent constitutes a violation. Pre-May-3-2013 conduct is evaluated under prior USPTO Code sections (e.g., 10.62, 10.65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of disciplined practitioner — 37 C.F.R. § 11.58
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligations imposed on a practitioner after discipline is imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes compliance obligations following exclusion or suspension. The Director’s order required compliance with §11.58 and specified administrative actions (dissociation from customer numbers, prohibition on obtaining customer numbers until reinstated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning criteria — 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors an ALJ must consider and explain when imposing exclusion or suspension: (1) duty violated (to client/public/legal system/profession), (2) mental state (intentional/knowing/negligent), (3) actual or potential injury caused, and (4) aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJ must analyze these factors (and may consult ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions) to justify severity of discipline (reprimand, suspension, exclusion). Examples: intentional fabrication weighs heavily as aggravating; prior conduct and harm to client’s patent rights are relevant to injury factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof in disciplinary proceedings — 37 C.F.R. § 11.49
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must prove violations of the USPTO Code or USPTO Rules by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings are evaluated against this evidentiary standard; admissions and documentary proof can satisfy it. Credibility findings that support such evidence are accorded deference on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedures to USPTO Director — 37 C.F.R. § 11.55 and § 11.56
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing appeals from an ALJ’s Initial Decision: appeal to Director within 30 days; Director may conduct de novo review and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand; reconsideration procedures and timing (e.g., 20 days for reconsideration per §11.56(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals must comply with filing requirements (brief format/timeliness); noncompliant briefs may be struck but parties may be permitted to amend. Director reviews record and has delegated authority to issue final order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative authority / Requests for Information (RFI) — 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may send Requests for Information and Evidence under §11.22(f) during investigation of practitioner conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to RFIs is part of the investigatory process; failure to provide accurate information can inform disciplinary charges. The investigation record (RFIs, responses, third-party evidence) is used by OED in charging decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of pre-2013 USPTO Code for earlier conduct — 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20-10.112 (e.g., 10.62, 10.65)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct before May 3, 2013 is evaluated under the earlier USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and its sections (e.g., prohibitions on employment creating impaired judgment, limits on business relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings may charge violations of both the old Code and current Rules depending on when the misconduct occurred; precedent under the old Code is relevant to assessing conflict-of-interest and business-transaction violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-practice procedural obligations as measures of competence/diligence (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.78(b); responding to Notices to File Missing Parts; petitions to revive; 30-month national fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO statutory/regulatory patent prosecution requirements — timely filing of drawings and documents, filing petitions under §1.78(b) to restore provisional priority when delay was unintentional, responding to Notices to File Missing Parts, paying national fees within 30 months, and filing petitions to revive abandoned applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with these patent-practice deadlines and procedural requirements (e.g., losing priority date due to untimely submission of drawings, failing to file required petitions or pay fees) can be evidence of incompetence, lack of diligence, and may cause substantial client harm used in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and professional-ethics authorities (ABA Model Rules R.1.8; ABA Formal Op. 00-418; USPTO precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: ABA Model Rules and ethics opinions, and prior USPTO disciplinary decisions, inform interpretation and application of USPTO ethics rules (e.g., business transaction disclosure and informed consent requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJs and the Director may cite ABA commentary and prior disciplinary cases (In re Lane, Haley, Watkins, etc.) to support findings that similar conduct warrants discipline; formal opinions support the requirement for written disclosure/consent when acquiring client interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility determinations and appellate deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings based on witness credibility by the ALJ are accorded substantial deference on review and are seldom overturned, particularly where the ALJ observed testimony and explained credibility conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review cites Anderson v. City of Bessemer and similar authorities recognizing that trial/ALJ credibility findings (demeanor, inconsistencies, admissions) are entitled to deference; a credible record-based explanation is important to sustaining factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions in assessing discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: ALJs may consult the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when evaluating appropriate discipline and weighing aggravating and mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standards structure sanction analysis (e.g., how intentionality, harm, prior discipline, and remorse bear on sanction choice) and are used alongside §11.54(b) factors to justify exclusion, suspension, or lesser penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner subject to USPTO disciplinary authority — 37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons registered to practice before the USPTO (e.g., patent attorneys/agents registered with USPTO) are subject to USPTO disciplinary authority and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration status brings a practitioner within the jurisdiction of OED and the ALJ process. Discipline can include exclusion from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline administrative orders and collateral administrative actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary orders may include administrative actions such as dissociation of practitioner’s name from USPTO Customer Numbers, prohibition on obtaining or being added to Customer Numbers until reinstated, and notice to state bars and courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions are not limited to practice suspension/exclusion; administrative restraints on electronic systems and notifications to other disciplinary/regulatory authorities are standard components of final orders.
